scope: Past Written Papers (PP) series retrieval index. One entry per paper and one per question. This file is an INDEX, not a content source: answer text lives only in the paper spec. Regenerate with build_index.py; never hand-edit.
naming_convention: QP<YY><MM>.html, where QP = Question Paper, YY = year and MM = month of the sitting (QP2607 = July 2026); question_id QP<YY><MM>-Q<n>; anchors #q1..#q9
source_of_truth_policy: specs/<PAPER>.json is authoritative for content. This manifest is authoritative for retrieval. Both index pages and the paper page are generated; editing generated HTML is always wrong.

recurrence_statuses.single: Set once in the sittings MIW has transcribed. NOT "never asked before".
recurrence_statuses.first: Earliest sitting of a family that returns at a later sitting.
recurrence_statuses.repeat_exact: Later sitting; normalised printed stem identical to the first.
recurrence_statuses.repeat_near: Later sitting; printed stem materially reworded.

recurrence_rule: Canonical recurrence is computed chronologically in recurrence_model.py from (year, month) over MIW's own transcriptions, and from nothing else. The source copy host's printed annotation is discovery-only provenance held in the spec as host_recurrence_hint and is never published; the authoring field recurrence_class records production order, not sitting order. Every count here is scoped to the sittings MIW has transcribed.

paper_status_model.available: Answers are published for this sitting.
paper_status_model.coming_later: No answers yet. Covers every case a student cannot act on -- not transcribed, in production, or source copy held only. Holding a source copy never reads as solved.

questions.question_text: Explain the principle of "Uberrimae Fidei" in Marine Insurance. What are the different disclosures which must be made by the insured to the insurer in Marine Insurance? List the circumstances which need not be disclosed to the insurer. What happens to the Marine Insurance contract if the disclosures are not made to the insurer at the time of the conclusion of the contract? (16)
questions.short_title: Uberrimae Fidei and Disclosure in Marine Insurance
questions.family_summary: First set here. The same task returns at July 2026 Q9.
questions.verification_status: Verified against the Indian statute for the January 2024 sitting. Marine Insurance Act, 1963 sections 19, 20(1) to 20(5), 21 and 22 were read as the operative text. The four exceptions at section 20(3) were taken as a closed list from the section itself, with the governing words "in the absence of enquiry" retained. The Act was confirmed unamended in these sections as at January 2024; no Indian case law was verified for this build and none is cited.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 is unamended in sections 19 to 22 as at the January 2024 sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. The statute is long-standing and no amendment to these sections was found, but the claim is date-bound and should be re-confirmed before publication rather than carried forward on the strength of this build.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The list of material circumstances typically disclosed is underwriting practice, not statutory text
reverify_before_publication.why: Stated in the answer as practice and labelled as such on the page. The Act states a test and does not enumerate. Recorded as an accepted limitation rather than promoted to a statutory list.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No Indian case law supports or qualifies the statutory propositions in this answer
reverify_before_publication.why: None was verified for this build. The answer rests on the sections alone, which is sufficient for the question as printed. If authority is later verified, the materiality discussion can be strengthened rather than corrected.

questions.question_text: a) Discuss the key provisions and objectives of the Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic (FAL Convention). (6) b) Briefly discuss the impact of the FAL Convention on enhancing efficiency and Security in international maritime traffic. (4) c) Discuss the significance of the FAL Convention in promoting global cooperation and standardization in maritime trade. (6)
questions.short_title: FAL Convention - Provisions, Impact and Significance
search_aliases: Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic
regulations: FAL Convention 1965 (adopted 9 April 1965, in force 5 March 1967)
FAL Convention Article VII(2)(b) - tacit acceptance
Resolution FAL.14(46) (13 May 2022, in force 1 January 2024)
Resolution FAL.15(47) (17 March 2023, in force 1 January 2025 - not in force at this sitting)
2016 FAL amendments (in force 1 January 2018; electronic exchange mandatory 9 April 2019)
IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business
questions.family_summary: Set once in the sittings MIW has transcribed.
questions.verification_status: Verified against the IMO's published account of the Convention and its amendment record. Adoption 9 April 1965 and entry into force 5 March 1967 were confirmed, as were the seven sections of the Annex, the Standards / Recommended Practices distinction and the notification duty. The amendment position was established specifically for this sitting: resolution FAL.14(46), adopted 13 May 2022, entered into force 1 January 2024 and makes single window systems mandatory; resolution FAL.15(47), adopted 17 March 2023, did not enter into force until 1 January 2025 and is therefore adopted but NOT in force at this sitting. The 2016 amendments, in force 1 January 2018, made electronic exchange of information mandatory from 9 April 2019. The Convention text itself was not held in the local corpus and is recorded as an accepted limitation.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Resolution FAL.14(46) entered into force on 1 January 2024 and is therefore operative at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: The load-bearing currency fact of the question, and the sitting falls in the first month of the new regime. Confirm the date has not been restated or corrected by IMO before publication, and confirm no later amendment is being back-read into this answer.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Resolution FAL.15(47) was adopted 17 March 2023 and did not enter into force until 1 January 2025, so it is not in force at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: A tacit-acceptance date can in principle be defeated by objection. Re-confirm the entry-into-force date before publication; the answer's value depends on the adopted-but-not-in-force distinction being exactly right.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Annex section list, the FAL Form titles and the Standards / Recommended Practices mechanism as stated
reverify_before_publication.why: Taken from the IMO's published account of the Convention, not from the consolidated instrument text, which is not held in the local corpus. Recorded as an accepted limitation; the answer quotes no Standard number that this source does not support.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No count of Standards and Recommended Practices is given
reverify_before_publication.why: Deliberate. The 2022 amendments followed a comprehensive review of the entire Annex, so any circulating pre-2024 count is unreliable. If a count is later verified against the instrument, it may be added; it must not be guessed.

questions.question_text: Explain the concept of CII rating and critically discuss the role of measuring metrics of AER and EEOI. What are the measures required to be taken by the vessel to improve its CII ratings. (16)
questions.short_title: CII Rating, AER and EEOI
regulations: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28 (Operational carbon intensity)
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 27 (fuel oil consumption data)
Resolution MEPC.328(76) - 2021 revised MARPOL Annex VI
Resolution MEPC.353(78) - CII Reference Lines Guidelines G2
Resolution MEPC.338(76) - CII Reduction Factors Guidelines G3
Resolution MEPC.354(78) - CII Rating Guidelines G4
Resolution MEPC.355(78) - CII Correction Factors and Voyage Adjustments G5
questions.family_summary: First set here. The same task returns at April 2025 Q6.
questions.verification_status: Verified against primary instruments read directly from the local True Source corpus. Regulation 28 of MARPOL Annex VI was read in full from resolution MEPC.328(76), the 2021 revised Annex VI, including the attained CII duty at 28.1 to 28.3, the required CII formula at 28.4 and 28.5, the rating at 28.6, the corrective-action and incentive provisions at 28.7 to 28.10 and the review at 28.11. Regulations 26 (SEEMP, including the Part III content required on or before 1 January 2023) and 27 (fuel oil consumption data collection from calendar year 2019) were read from the same resolution. The reduction factor table was taken verbatim from MEPC.338(76) (G3). The AER, cgDIST and EEOI definitions and the capacity assignments by ship type were taken verbatim from MEPC.352(78) (G1), sections 2, 4 and 5. The rating framework and the five grades were taken from MEPC.354(78) (G4). The voyage adjustment and correction factor definitions were taken from MEPC.355(78) (G5). Every guideline consulted is the edition in force at the January 2024 sitting. Post-sitting instruments held in the corpus - MEPC 81 of March 2024 and MEPC 82 of October 2024 - were deliberately excluded.

reverify_before_publication.claim: At the January 2024 sitting no ship had yet been assigned a CII rating, 2023 being the first calculation year with reports due by 31 March 2024
reverify_before_publication.why: The load-bearing sitting-relative statement in the answer. It is derived from regulations 28.1 and 28.2 and is correct as at the sitting, but it is exactly the kind of statement that a later editor would silently modernise. Confirm it is still stated in the past-tense sitting frame before publication.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The reduction factor Z for 2024 is 7 % and the factors for 2027 to 2030 were not set at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: Taken verbatim from G3 table 1 as it stood. The regulation 28.11 review was empowered to revise Z, so a later amendment may change the table. The answer must continue to state the position as at January 2024, not the current one.

THE PRINTED PHRASE 'TWIN SKEG DESIGN' IS AMBIGUOUS and the answer states which reading it takes - the twin-screw twin-skeg arrangement - rather than resolving it silently. Energy saving devices are expressly distinguished from hull form rather than blurred into aftbody optimisation. Nothing from MEPC 81, which sat five weeks after this examination, appears anywhere. questions.verification_status: PRIMARY, READ AT SOURCE THIS SESSION. Regulation VIII/1, Regulation VIII/2 and Section A-VIII/1 of the STCW Convention and Code were read in full from the STCW Consolidated Edition 2017 held in the MIW True Source corpus at official-sources/STCW-2017.pdf. That PDF carries NO TEXT LAYER, so the provisions were read by rendering the pages and reading the rendered images - Convention Chapter VIII and Code Chapter VIII Section A-VIII/1 in their entirety. Every number in this answer - 10 hours in 24, 77 hours in 7, two periods with one of at least 6 hours, the 14-hour interval, the 70-hour exception floor, the three-period and one-hour exception limits, the two-consecutive-week limit, the two 24-hour periods in any 7-day period, and the 0.05% BAC / 0.25 mg/l breath limit - was read off the printed provision, not recalled. AMENDMENT STATE CHECKED FOR THIS SITTING: the operative text is the 2017 consolidated edition as amended by MSC.416/417(97) (in force 1 July 2018) and MSC.486/487(103) (in force 1 January 2023), both before this sitting; MSC.560(108) is adopted but does not enter into force until 1 January 2026 and is Chapter VI in any event; the HTW comprehensive review of STCW is in progress and is described as such, never as law.

questions.question_text: Explain the role of the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in promoting global sustainability. Choose any two SDGs and discuss their relevance to the maritime sector, highlighting specific actions the shipping industry can take to support their achievement. (16)

regulations: UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/70/1 (25 September 2015)

Hong Kong International Convention 2009 - not in force at this sitting
questions.family_summary: Set once in the sittings MIW has transcribed.
questions.verification_status: Verified against primary sources at the December 2024 sitting date. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly by resolution A/RES/70/1 on 25 September 2015 and came into effect on 1 January 2016, comprising 17 Sustainable Development Goals and 169 targets, organised around the five areas of People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership, with the central pledge to leave no one behind; progress is reviewed through the High-Level Political Forum and voluntary national reviews, and measured against a global indicator framework. The maritime limb was anchored instrument by instrument at the sitting date. The operative IMO climate instrument is the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, resolution MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023, which superseded the 2018 Initial Strategy: net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around, i.e. close to, 2050; indicative checkpoints for 2030 and 2040; and uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and energy sources by 2030. The short-term measures - EEXI, the operational CII and the enhanced SEEMP - entered into force 1 January 2023, so 2023 is the first full CII data year and the first ratings were issued during 2024. MEPC 82, held 30 September to 4 October 2024, continued work on the mid-term measures and opened the review of the short-term measures, referring it to a correspondence group and an intersessional working group reporting to MEPC 83 in 2025; NO mid-term measure had been adopted at this sitting and none is described as adopted. For SDG 14 the instruments relied on are MARPOL Annexes I to VI, the Ballast Water Management Convention 2004 (in force 8 September 2017), the AFS Convention 2001, and the London Convention and Protocol. The Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships, 2009 was verified separately: its entry-into-force criteria were met in June 2023 when Bangladesh and Liberia became Contracting States, and it enters into force 24 months later on 26 JUNE 2025 - which is SIX MONTHS AFTER this examination, so at this sitting it is adopted and ratified but NOT YET IN FORCE, and the answer says so expressly.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, resolution MEPC.377(80) of 7 July 2023, is the operative strategy at this sitting, having superseded the 2018 Initial Strategy
reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. Do not revert to the 2018 Initial Strategy, and do not advance to any later strategy or measure. The 2023 Strategy is correct for December 2024.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No IMO mid-term GHG measure had been adopted at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT ADD ONE. The mid-term measures were under development and the work was referred onward to MEPC 83 in 2025, after this examination. An editor working from current material would find measures adopted and would introduce a state of affairs that did not exist at the sitting.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Hong Kong International Convention 2009 was adopted and ratified but NOT YET IN FORCE at this sitting, entering into force 26 June 2025
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT UPDATE THIS. The Convention entered into force six months AFTER this examination. Current material describes it as in force; changing it here would destroy the adopted-versus-in-force point the answer is built on and would be wrong for a December 2024 sitting.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no figure is asserted for shipping's share of global greenhouse gas emissions or of world trade
reverify_before_publication.why: Both figures circulate very widely and are quoted at materially different values by different sources and study years. None was verified for this sitting and the argument is deliberately made qualitatively. If a figure is added later it must be sourced and dated at or before December 2024.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The numerical values of the 2030 and 2040 indicative checkpoints in the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy are described in structure rather than quoted
reverify_before_publication.why: The checkpoint values were not re-read from the resolution text in this session. The structure - a percentage reduction in total annual GHG emissions against a 2008 baseline, stated as a minimum with a higher striving-for level - IS established, as are the net-zero-by-or-around-2050 and 2030 zero or near-zero fuel ambitions. If the figures are added later they must come from MEPC.377(80) itself.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no SDG progress statistic or count of voluntary national reviews is asserted
reverify_before_publication.why: UN progress reporting is published annually and none was verified for December 2024.

questions.verification_status: Verified against primary sources. Resolution MSC.337(91), Code on noise levels on board ships, adopted 30 November 2012, was obtained and read in full - the resolution's operative paragraphs including the statement that the Code takes effect on 1 July 2014 upon entry into force of SOLAS regulation II-1/3-12; the preamble; chapter 1 (1.1 scope, 1.1.3 the list of provisions that remain recommendatory, 1.2 purpose, 1.3 application including the eleven excluded ship types at 1.3.4 and the dispensation power at 1.3.6, and the definitions at 1.4); chapter 4 (4.1 general including the 85 dB(A) and 110 dB(A) statements, and the complete 4.2 noise level limits table in both tonnage columns, and 4.3 the survey report); chapter 5 (5.1 the Lex(24) 80 dB(A) design criterion and the 135 dB(C) peak limit, 5.2, 5.3 zones A to E, 5.4 the 24-hour alternative and the four-hour/eight-hour daily limits, 5.5 the hearing conservation programme); chapter 6 (6.2.1 the four sound reduction index values and 6.3.2 the 3 dB field tolerance); and chapter 7 (7.2.2 hearing protectors to reduce to 85 dB(A) or less, and 7.4 the four warning notice bands). Resolution MSC.338(91), adopted 30 November 2012 and in force 1 July 2014, was read in full for SOLAS regulation II-1/3-12 - the three application date criteria at paragraph 1, the retro-fit style requirement for the 2009-2015 build window at paragraph 2, the mandatory-instrument statement at paragraph 3, the exclusion cross-reference at paragraph 4, and the consequential deletion of the former regulation II-1/36. Every dB figure, date and paragraph number in the answer was checked against those two texts.

reverify_before_publication.why: SOLAS II-1/3-12.3 expressly contemplates amendment of the Code by the Organization. No amendment was identified as at this sitting, and the regulation text is taken from its adopting resolution rather than a licensed consolidated SOLAS. If an amendment is later found to have taken effect before December 2024, the limits and application provisions must be re-checked against it.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The text of SOLAS regulation II-1/3-12
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW holds no licensed IMO consolidated SOLAS edition. The regulation is taken from resolution MSC.338(91), which is a sound source for the regulation as adopted but would not reflect any subsequent amendment to it.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The description of zones A to E in chapter 5
reverify_before_publication.why: Figure 1 of the Code is a graph of level against duration and cannot be tabulated without loss. The answer gives the numerical anchors the figure carries and describes the zones rather than redrawing it.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no epidemiological statistic on noise-induced hearing loss among seafarers is asserted
reverify_before_publication.why: The health effects stated are those the Code itself identifies together with generally accepted occupational-health mechanism. No prevalence study was verified for this sitting; if a figure is added later it must be sourced and dated at or before December 2024.

questions.verification_status: Verified against the Paris MoU's published procedures and against authoritative industry guidance, anchored to the December 2024 sitting. The New Inspection Regime entered into force on 1 January 2011, replacing the previous target factor with a ship risk profile and replacing the 25 per cent individual inspection commitment with a shared commitment to inspect all ships visiting the region. The Ship Risk Profile parameters, the three risk categories, the periodic inspection windows (High Risk 5 to 6 months, Standard Risk 10 to 12 months, Low Risk 24 to 36 months), the Priority I and Priority II definitions, the overriding and unexpected factor triggers, the inspection types and the expanded-inspection population (every High Risk Ship, and every bulk carrier, chemical tanker, gas carrier, oil tanker or passenger ship older than 12 years), the ETA72, ETA24, ATA and ATD reporting obligations, the THETIS database fed through SafeSeaNet, and the refusal-of-access criteria and durations (black-listed flag banned after the third detention in 36 months; grey-listed flag after the third detention in 24 months; any detention after the second ban; lifting after 3 months, 12 months, 24 months, then permanent) were all established from those sources. Sitting-date position verified separately: the performance lists operative at this examination are the 2023 lists, approved at the 57th Committee meeting and applied from 1 July 2024; the Russian Federation is suspended from the Paris MoU; and the Ship Risk Profile revisions aligned with the recast EU Port State Control Directive were still in preparation, that Directive applying from 2027, so they are recorded as future and not as operative.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The 2023 Paris MoU performance lists, applied from 1 July 2024, are the White, Grey and Black Lists operative at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: The lists are recalculated from a three-year rolling period and reissued each July. A later editor working from current Paris MoU material would find a different set described as current. The sitting-date lists are the 2023 lists and must not be advanced.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The revised Ship Risk Profile aligned with the recast EU Port State Control Directive, including environmental criteria, was NOT operative at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT ADD ENVIRONMENTAL PARAMETERS TO THE PROFILE. The recast Directive applies from 2027 and the revised methodologies were in preparation at this sitting. Current Paris MoU material will describe them as adopted or in force; introducing them would be future contamination in a December 2024 paper.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Russian Federation is suspended from the Paris MoU at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. Guidance issued at the NIR's introduction lists the Russian Federation as a full member and describes its national system as feeding THETIS; that description is stale and must not be reinstated.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No numerical weighting from Table 1 of Annex 7 is asserted anywhere in this answer
reverify_before_publication.why: The weighting table could not be retrieved from the Paris MoU's own published source by automated means. A fabricated or half-remembered weighting would be worse than none. If the table is later obtained, weightings may be added - but they must come from the Memorandum itself and must be the version in force at December 2024.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Paris MoU membership is stated as 27 maritime authorities with the Russian Federation suspended, and no count of active members is asserted
reverify_before_publication.why: Suspension does not remove membership and the organisation's own presentation retains the suspended State in the list. Any figure for active members would be an inference rather than a record.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No per-flag listing, detention rate or inspection count is asserted
reverify_before_publication.why: The lists move annually and no per-flag position was verified for this sitting. If a figure is added later it must be the position as at or before December 2024.

questions.verification_status: Verified against the December 2024 sitting date. The operative edition of the Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification at this sitting is resolution A.1186(33), HSSC 2023, adopted 6 December 2023, which revokes A.1156(32). That edition was established for this sitting independently, from the 33rd Assembly boundary of 6 December 2023 recorded in the paper anchor, and cross-checked against the donor QP2509-Q9, which read A.1186(33) directly and quoted annex sections 4.2, 4.3 and 4.4 verbatim. The annual survey definition and frequency, the periodical survey's two different frequencies and its attachment to only the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificates, and the intermediate survey frequency are taken from those sections. Resolution A.1207(34), adopted 3 December 2025, post-dates this examination by twelve months and appears nowhere in this object except as an express future-instrument warning. The RO Code is MSC.349(92) with MEPC.237(65), not MSC.349(90); that correction is carried forward from the donor chain and re-checked. SOLAS regulation wording rests on authoritative secondary reproduction - MIW holds no licensed IMO consolidated SOLAS edition - and that limitation is recorded.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Resolution A.1186(33), adopted 6 December 2023, is the operative edition of the Survey Guidelines under the HSSC AT THIS SITTING
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT UPDATE THIS. The Guidelines are re-adopted roughly every two years and A.1186(33) was superseded by A.1207(34) on 3 December 2025 - TWO YEARS AFTER this examination. The sitting-date citation is A.1186(33) and it is correct. A later editor working from current IMO material will find A.1186(33) described as revoked and may 'correct' it; that would introduce future contamination into a December 2024 paper. The study guide, the major_trap and retrieval card C9 all warn against this expressly. Note also that the June 2026 member of this question family, QP2606-Q8, correctly cites A.1207(34) for ITS sitting - do not harmonise the two objects.

questions.verification_status: Verified against primary and authoritative sources at the December 2024 sitting date. The regulatory anchor is the Code of the International Standards and Recommended Practices for a Safety Investigation into a Marine Casualty or Marine Incident (Casualty Investigation Code), adopted by resolution MSC.255(84) in 2008, Parts I and II of which were made mandatory by amendments to SOLAS chapter XI-1 inserting regulation XI-1/6, effective 1 January 2010. The Code's central principle - that a marine safety investigation is conducted to prevent future casualties and is separate and distinct from, and must not seek to apportion, blame or determine liability - was established from the Code itself, as was the requirement to conduct a safety investigation into every VERY SERIOUS MARINE CASUALTY, defined as one involving the total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment. questions.family_summary: Set once in the sittings MIW has transcribed.
questions.verification_status: Verified against the conventions and the Indian implementing statutes as at the December 2024 sitting. The Hague Rules 1924 and the Hague-Visby Rules (the 1968 Visby Protocol and the 1979 SDR Protocol) were used for the definition of 'carriage of goods' as covering the period from the time when the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship (Article I(e)); the carrier's obligations of due diligence to make the ship seaworthy before and at the beginning of the voyage and properly and carefully to load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods (Article III rules 1 and 2); the catalogue of exceptions (Article IV rule 2(a) to (q)) including the nautical fault and fire exceptions, perils of the sea, inherent defect quality or vice of the goods, insufficiency of packing, latent defects not discoverable by due diligence, and the catch-all at (q) with its burden of proof on the carrier; the package or unit limitation as amended by the Visby and SDR Protocols; and the one-year time bar under Article III rule 6. The Hamburg Rules 1978 were used for the port-to-port period of responsibility (Article 4) and the presumed-fault basis of liability (Article 5). The Rotterdam Rules 2008 were used for the door-to-door period (Articles 11 and 12) and are recorded as ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE at this sitting. The Indian position at this sitting was established as: the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925, amended in 1993 to give effect to the Hague-Visby Rules, together with the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856; India is not a party to the Hamburg Rules or the Rotterdam Rules. No post-2024 Indian carriage legislation appears anywhere in this object.

reverify_before_publication.claim: At the December 2024 sitting the governing Indian statutes are the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 as amended in 1993, and the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT ADVANCE THESE. India's carriage and bills of lading legislation was subsequently replaced. A later editor working from current Indian law would substitute the replacement statutes and would introduce law that did not exist at this sitting. This is the same boundary that keeps the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 rather than the MS Act 2025 throughout this paper.

reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. The status is stated rather than a ratification count, precisely so the claim does not become fragile - but if the Convention later enters into force, this object must NOT be updated, because the answer is correct for December 2024.

reverify_before_publication.why: Those figures move. The answer asserts status, not counts - Rotterdam not in force, Hamburg in force but not adopted by the major maritime trading nations. If a count is added later it must be the position as at or before December 2024.

Resolution A.1187(33), the 2023 Non-exhaustive list of obligations, adopted 6 December 2023, was re-read directly for the instrument list, the mandatory-application chain and its annex structure; its Annex 7 window (1 January to 1 July 2024) is CLOSED at this sitting and the answer states it as retrospective, which reverses the framing correct for a January 2024 paper. Every paragraph number in the answer was checked against the source text. The operative Assembly editions at this sitting are the A.11xx(33) series adopted 6 December 2023; no A.12xx(34) instrument appears anywhere in this object.

reverify_before_publication.claim: A.1070(28) is unamended and is the III Code operative at the December 2024 sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. The Assembly may amend the Code on the recommendation of MSC and MEPC under operative paragraph 2. Confirm no amendment took effect before December 2024 and that none is being back-read into the answer.

reverify_before_publication.claim: A.1187(33) of 6 December 2023 is the operative Non-exhaustive list of obligations at this sitting, having revoked A.1157(32), and its Annex 7 window is CLOSED
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT REVERSE THIS TO THE JANUARY 2024 FRAMING. A solved January 2024 paper in this same family correctly describes Annex 7 as forward-looking, because at that sitting the 1 January to 1 July 2024 window lay ahead. At December 2024 it has closed. An editor cross-reading the two papers may 'harmonise' them and would reintroduce a wrong statement about what is in force.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The A.11xx(33) series adopted 6 December 2023 is the operative Assembly material at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: The 34th Assembly adopted its resolutions on 3 December 2025, a full year after this examination. No A.12xx(34) instrument may be introduced into this object by a later editor working from current IMO material.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The audit scope is commonly summarised as nine mandatory IMO instruments
reverify_before_publication.why: Stated in the answer as a common summary, not as a quotation. Neither A.1070(28) nor A.1187(33) states a number. If a source that does state one is later located, replace the hedged wording with the cited figure.

reverify_before_publication.claim: IMSAS uses the III Code as its audit standard
reverify_before_publication.why: Established from the mandatory-application chain recited in A.1070(28) and A.1187(33), both read. The Framework and Procedures resolution itself was not re-read, so no claim about periodicity or audit procedure is made.

questions.verification_status: The governing IMO material was read in full at source. CCC.1/Circ.2 of 20 October 2015 and its successor CCC.1/Circ.2/Rev.1 of 20 September 2017 were both obtained from IMO and read; Rev.1 expressly supersedes the original. The particle-size criteria that separate the two bauxite schedules are taken from Annex 1 of Rev.1 - the Test Procedure for Determining the TML for Bauxite as finalized by CCC 4 - which states them numerically, so the criteria are primary rather than secondary. The amendment history - amendment 05-19, resolution MSC.462(101), mandatory 1 January 2021 - is corroborated by two independent authoritative sources. reverify_before_publication.claim: IMSBC Code amendment 07-23 is the edition mandatory at this sitting, and amendment 08-25 had no application
reverify_before_publication.why: The IMSBC Code runs a two-year amendment cycle. 07-23 became mandatory 1 January 2025 and 08-25 becomes mandatory 1 January 2027, applying voluntarily from 1 January 2026. Both boundaries are outside this sitting and the sitting-date position is secure. Confirm the present position separately without altering the answer.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The indicative moisture limit of 10% is presented ONLY as superseded history

reverify_before_publication.why: MIW holds no licensed IMSBC Code, so the individual schedules have not been read in the Code itself. The groups and the criteria are established from IMO circular CCC.1/Circ.2/Rev.1 and its annexed test procedure, corroborated by two independent authoritative sources. Re-verify against a licensed IMSBC Code before publication.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No TML value, stowage factor or angle of repose for bauxite appears anywhere in this object

regulations: NO REGULATORY INSTRUMENT PRESCRIBES THIS ANSWER. Recorded deliberately under PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL.md section 2.1 - an invented regulation number would be a far worse defect than an openly declared engineering-judgement answer.

questions.verification_status: Answered under the section 2.1 technical-source policy: no instrument prescribes the answer and none has been invented. MAN Energy Solutions' 'Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion' was obtained from man-es.com and READ DIRECTLY this session, and it is the source of every quantity given. Verified from it: the light running margin defined as LRM = (nL - nH) / nH x 100 per cent, with MAN's own recommendation of 4 to 7 per cent depending on the specific ship and operational profile and up to 10 per cent in special cases; the rule of thumb that a 20 per cent increase in required power from added resistance corresponds to about 1 per cent heavy running, that is 1 per cent lower rpm for the same engine power; the engine load diagram limit lines, in particular that LINE 4 IS THE TORQUE/SPEED LIMIT, LIMITED MAINLY BY THE THERMAL LOAD ON THE ENGINE, that line 5 is the maximum mean effective pressure for continuous operation and is a limit only at high loads and speeds while at lower speeds line 4 is the stricter limit, that line 6 is the light propeller curve for clean hull and calm weather, and that line 8 is the overload limit permitting overload running only for limited periods, one hour per twelve hours or when required in an emergency; that class rules generally do not allow an engine to run faster than 115 per cent of SMCR rpm; that frictional resistance increases with fouling of the hull by algae, sea grass and barnacles; that shallow water in general has no influence when the water depth is more than ten times the ship's draught; and that in the bollard pull condition a heavy running factor of 15 to 20 per cent relative to the light propeller curve has been experienced, equivalent to approximately a 60 to 100 per cent increase in power for the same rpm. Sea margin is recorded as typically 10 to 30 per cent with 15 per cent historically applied, and engine margin typically 10 to 30 per cent with 10 per cent historically applied, both from the same document.

questions.short_title: Casualty Investigation Code and VSMC
questions.family_summary: Returns reworded from June 2025 Q7. Also set at January 2026 Q8.
questions.verification_status: Reuse of the January verified answer after a question-delta and currency review at the April sitting date, with the Code re-read at source. Confirmed again in the text of MSC.255(84): paragraph 2.22 defines a very serious marine casualty as a marine casualty involving the total loss of the ship or a death or severe damage to the environment; paragraph 2.19 defines severe damage to the environment as damage which, as evaluated by the State(s) affected or the flag State, produces a major deleterious effect upon the environment - it is an evaluative test and NOT a tonnage threshold; paragraph 2.18 defines serious injury by incapacitation for more than 72 hours commencing within seven days; chapter 6.1 requires an investigation into every very serious marine casualty; and the preamble records the flag State duties in SOLAS regulation I/21, Load Lines Article 23 and MARPOL Article 12, with SOLAS XI-1/6 making Parts I and II mandatory from 1 January 2010 by MSC.257(84).

THE QUESTION'S FRAMING INVITES A FALSE STATEMENT, AND THE ANSWER DOES NOT MAKE IT.
